item.title: The Storage View Of KV Cache: Characterizing Cache Behavior Across LLM Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2611.10178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern LLM serving increasingly extends KV caches beyond GPU memory into host DRAM, SSDs, and remote storage, yet these stores remain largely governed by workload-agnostic policies such as LRU and fixed TTLs. We ask what execution context is needed by storage to make retention, reclamation, and placement decisions across heterogeneous workloads. We characterize KV-cache reuse, lifetime, and footprint at block granularity across 11 production and public traces spanning chat, API serving, RAG, coding agents, tool-using agents, and multi-lineage workflows. We examine reuse sources, recurrence timing and frequency, useful lifetimes, and storage consumption. Across workloads, KV state takes two recurring forms. Single-session state is reused within one execution: its footprint grows as sessions deepen and accumulates across concurrent sessions; it can remain useful through long idle periods but loses value at session completion. Multi-session state recurs across sessions of the same workload, outlives individual sessions, and spans hot prefixes and a large infrequent tail. While prior systems often exploit application-, agent-, or workflow-specific knowledge, our results suggest that three generic signals (a workload identifier, a session identifier, and session completion) expose much of the structure needed for KV-storage management. Trace-driven comparisons show that workload-specific recurrence estimates retain up to 22% more within-session hits and reduce dead state by up to 40%; a session completion signal eliminates the fundamental idle-time reclamation tradeoff for single-session state; and session-aware reuse classification identifies shared state 4-700x more selectively than request-level access counts. These results motivate a small cross-layer interface for workload-aware KV storage without application-specific semantics.
item.dc:creator: Talia Q. Chen, Daniel Waddington, Narangerelt Batsoyol, Vijay Chidambaram

item.title: Retention Horizons of Volatile Stores in iOS and Android Extractions
item.description: arXiv:2611.10309v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Whether an extraction can answer a question about a given day depends on how far back each store reaches, yet public statements rest on single test devices. We measured the retention horizon, the time from a store's oldest retained record to acquisition, for eight iOS and seven Android stores on 48 full file system extractions and seven bug reports, keeping devices whose clock agreed with the acquisition time (26 Apple devices, 13 Android phones). Horizons ranged from minutes to years and followed the mechanism that bounds each store. The unified log Persist stream reached a median of 2.5 days; interactionC reached 166 to 170 days on 18 of 25 devices. Android stores stayed within their source-code limits (usage statistics 10.2 days, DropBox 3.1, notifications 1.5); bug-report logs reached 3.1 hours at most. The oldest record misled three times: one knowledgeC stream reached back two years, the others a median of 29 days; interactionC read without its write-ahead log showed older records on 18 of 25 devices; and four of seven bug reports began with stray lines up to 16.6 days old above a body of 3.1 hours or less. A horizon belongs to a store, a release and a device.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kwaku Ntiamoah Addai, Sanders Larweh Tetteh, Selorm Adjabeng, Kingsley Albert Egyir

item.title: Device-Life Boundary Indicators and the Classification of Restored Versus Native Records on Android
item.description: arXiv:2611.10312v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A phone that shows calls, messages and photographs from years ago may have been set up recently and carried them over from an earlier handset, so its screen dates do not date the device's own life. Which traces fix where that life begins, how well they agree and how much of what is visible predates it is unmeasured. We read 14 Android full file system extractions (12 Samsung; Android 10 to 16), seven bug reports and 33 iOS extractions (a probe). Every Android device recorded a first boot, but the first evidence of user setup came a median of 98 days later (0 to 563). Of the 13 devices with messages, 7 held some dated before the first boot, a majority of them on 5; 24% of the apps outside the system image were installed as restored. Against the creator field that a migration tool leaves on messages, a boundary at user setup recalled all but 1 of 46,968 such messages, the first-boot boundary 94 to 100%. On synthetic fixtures, the labelling error followed the boundary error. A date on a record dates the device only once the record is shown to have been created on it.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kwaku Ntiamoah Addai, Selorm Adjabeng, Kingsley Albert Egyir, Sanders Larweh Tetteh

item.title: BunshinRL: Splitting Live Agent Workspaces for Memory-Efficient Agentic RL
item.description: arXiv:2611.10453v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
item.dc:creator: Yutong Huang, Vikranth Srivatsa, Alex Asch, Yiying Zhang

item.title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.11739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. A platform-side remedy cannot contain it: kubelet, given full disk-pressure visibility, frees 0 bytes and evicts 26 bystander pods, because its reclamation actuator is keyed to an accounting that does not know the cache exists. The article then eliminates the failure class inside the component that owns the bytes, with no change to kubelet or the container runtime interface, by two design rules: a byte budget whose pressure signal is keyed to filesystem truth, so that a never-blocking, lossy accounting still enforces a hard bound (held against about 301,000 dropped updates), and pass-through semantics under which a failed cache write never becomes a failed read, with the coupling traced to a single io.MultiWriter. Across six pre-specified campaigns on AWS, upstream stargz-snapshotter fails 273 of 280 model files at 90% cache pre-fill; the proposed system reads all 150.3 GB with zero errors at +18.5% completion cost and holds the budget under a live read, co-tenancy, and a three-node fleet. A source audit shows the missing bound generalizes to SOCI and Nydus. The implementation is open source and has been proposed upstream.
item.dc:creator: Georgii Kliukovkin
